entries.meaning: ‘Look upon me, lotus-eyed Lord; your gracious glance frees from sorrow. Dark as a blue lotus, Hari is the bee drinking nectar from the heart-lotus of Shiva, the enemy of desire; breaker of demon armies and their power, delighter of sages and good people, destroyer of sin; fresh cloud-bank for the crop of Brahmins, refuge of the shelterless and champion of the lowly; by your immense arm-strength Earth's burden was broken, and you are expert in slaying Khara, Dushana and Viradha; enemy of Ravana, embodiment of joy, finest king—victory to the full moon of Dasharatha's water-lily lineage. Your fair fame is known in Purana, Veda and Agama and sung in assemblies of gods, sages and saints. Compassionate one, breaker of false pride, all-skilled ornament of Kosala; crusher of Kali's impurity, whose name destroys possessiveness—Lord of Tulsidas, protect your suppliant.’

Shiva said, ‘Girija, hear this lucid account. I have told it all as far as my understanding permits. Rama's deeds are boundless—hundreds of millions; revelation and Sarasvati cannot reach the end of their description. Rama is infinite: infinite are his virtues, births, deeds and names. Drops of water and grains of earth may be counted, but Raghupati's deeds cannot be fully told. This stainless story bestows Hari's feet; hearing it gives unwavering devotion. Uma, I have related the lovely account that Bhushundi told the lord of birds. I have described a little of Rama's virtues; now tell me, Bhavani, what else I should say.’ Hearing the auspicious account, Uma rejoiced and spoke with great humility and tenderness: ‘Blessed, blessed—blessed am I, O enemy of Tripura! I have heard Rama's virtues, which remove the fear of becoming.’

‘Those who become satiated while hearing Rama's deeds have not known their distinctive flavour. Even great sages liberated while living hear Hari's virtues without cease. For one who wishes to cross the ocean of becoming, Rama's story is a sturdy ship; for the sensually absorbed, the host of Hari's virtues is pleasant to the ear and enchanting to the mind. Who in the world possesses ears yet does not find Raghupati's deeds lovely? Those inert creatures are destroyers of their own true selves who take no delight in Raghupati's story. You have sung the Manasa of Hari's deeds; hearing it, Master, I have found measureless joy. This lovely account that you told was sung by Kaka Bhushundi to Garuda.’

‘Listen, enemy of Tripura: among a thousand people perhaps one observes dharma and vows; among ten million people of righteous conduct perhaps one turns from sense-objects and delights in dispassion. Among ten million dispassionate people, revelation says, scarcely one gains right knowledge; among ten million who possess knowledge, scarcely one in the world becomes liberated while living. Among a thousand such people, the realized one absorbed in Brahman—the mine of every joy—is hard to find. People of righteous conduct, dispassion and knowledge, those liberated while living and intent on Brahman: rarer than them all, lord of gods, is one devoted to Rama, beyond pride and Maya. How did a crow obtain that devotion to Hari? Lord of the universe, explain it to me.’

‘Compassionate Lord, tell me where the crow obtained this sacred, lovely account of the Lord's deeds. How did you hear it, enemy of desire? Tell me, for my wonder is immense. Garuda is profoundly wise, a treasury of virtues, Hari's servant who dwells very near him. Why did he leave hosts of sages and go to a crow to hear the story? Tell me how the dialogue between the two devotees of Hari—the crow and the serpent-eater—came about.’ Hearing Gauri's straightforward, lovely speech, Shiva answered reverently and joyfully: ‘Blessed are you, Sati, and holy is your understanding; your love for Raghupati's feet is no small thing. Hear this supremely sacred history: upon hearing it all worldly delusion vanishes, trust in Rama's feet arises, and a person crosses the ocean of becoming without effort.’

‘Fair-faced, lovely-eyed one, hear the circumstances in which I heard this story that frees from worldly existence. Your first incarnation was in Daksha's house, when your name was Sati. When insult occurred at Daksha's sacrifice, in great anger you gave up your life. My attendants broke up the sacrifice; you know that whole episode. Then tremendous grief arose in my heart, and I suffered in separation from you, my beloved. Dispassionately I wandered, viewing beautiful forests, mountains, rivers and ponds as curiosities. Far north of Mount Sumeru stands a very lovely blue mountain. Its four delightful golden peaks pleased my mind. On each grew a vast tree—a banyan, a pipal, a pakari and a mango. Atop the mountain a lovely lake shone, its gem-built steps captivating my mind.’

‘On that lovely mountain lives that very bird, who is not destroyed even at the end of a kalpa. The many qualities and faults made by Maya—delusion, desire and other forms of ignorance—pervade the whole world, yet never approach that mountain. Uma, hear with devotion how the crow dwells there and worships Hari. Beneath the pipal he meditates; beneath the pakari he performs repetition and sacrifice; in the mango's shade he offers mental worship—apart from worshipping Hari, he has no other occupation. Beneath the banyan he tells episodes from Hari's story. Many birds come and listen as he reverently sings Rama's wondrous deeds in many forms with love. All the pure-minded swans that live continually on that lake hear him. When I went and saw this marvel, exceptional bliss arose in my heart.’

‘Girija, I have told the whole history of the occasion on which I went to the bird. Now hear why Garuda, banner of the bird race, went to the crow. When Raghunatha enacted warfare, I feel embarrassment when I consider that deed: he allowed himself to be bound by Indrajit's serpent weapon, and sage Narada sent Garuda. The serpent-eater cut the bonds and departed, but fierce despondency arose in his heart. As the enemy of serpents pondered the Lord's bondage in many ways, he thought: “He is all-pervading Brahman, the stainless Lord of speech, the Supreme Lord beyond Maya and delusion. I had heard that he incarnated in the world, yet I have seen nothing of such power.”’

He tried to reason with his mind in many ways, but knowledge did not dawn and delusion covered his heart. Distressed, wearied and multiplying arguments, he fell under delusion just as you once did. Troubled, he went to the divine sage Narada and stated the doubt within his mind. Hearing him, Narada felt great compassion: ‘Listen, bird: Rama's Maya is mighty. It steals even the minds of the wise, forcibly bewildering them. The very Maya that has made me dance many times has now pervaded you too, lord of birds. Great delusion has arisen in your heart; my words alone will not quickly remove it. Go to four-faced Brahma, lord of birds, and do whatever he directs.’

The lord of birds then went to Brahma and began relating his doubt. On hearing it, Brahma bowed his head to Rama; remembering Rama's power, he was deeply immersed in love. The Creator reflected inwardly: ‘When poet, scholar and sage alike are subject to Maya—Hari's Maya has boundless power and has made even me dance many times—what wonder is there in the bird-king's delusion, when the moving and unmoving universe is pervaded by it and the world is my offspring?’ Then Brahma spoke lovely words: ‘Mahesha knows Rama's majesty. Son of Vinata, go to Shiva and ask no one else. There your doubt will be destroyed.’ Hearing Brahma's words, the bird departed.
